title: Wrap-up
text:
Four problems, four patterns

Productive workflows — the friction between you and the render
Design once, use anywhere — one brand, every format
Build reusable structures — the boilerplate around your content
Why Typst matters — a PDF you can restyle


Each one stands alone. Pick up the ones that match what you already fight with.

title: Wrap-up
text:
Which piece for which job?

_brand.yml — the same look across formats and projects. One repo, not a theme per project.
Template partials — the same structure, different content. Format specific, and driven by metadata.


Look, structure, distribution. Three different problems.
Reach for the smallest piece that solves yours.

title: Wrap-up
section: What we did not get to
text:
What we did not get to
Lua filters — change the document while Pandoc holds it as an AST.
Not format specific, so one filter can serve html, typst, and revealjs. Reach for one when the change you want is to the content, not the boilerplate around it.
Extending Quarto → — a whole workshop on filters, shortcodes, and extensions

Partials are the boilerplate. Filters are the content.
That workshop’s materials are open, same license as these.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
What is a template?
You write a document.


Title in the YAML, one line of markdown.
Teal is yours.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
What is a template?
Render it, and you get an HTML document.


Only the teal came from the document. Where does the other stuff come from?

title: Build reusable structures
text:
What is a template?
A template: boilerplate, with named holes.


The template provides the boilerplate: with named holes for your content. E.g. $title$ takes a value from the YAML by name. — the mechanism the next hour rests on.
Notice $body$ is your content translated. Pandoc did that.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
What is a partial?
Part of the template renders the title block.


Same file as the previous slide, grown a little.
There’s a chunk that has one job, make the title block.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
What is a partial?
Pull it out into its own file, now its a partial.


That gets pulled out into it’s own file and referenced in the template. It’s called a partial, and inside looks just like a template, HTML boilerplate with holes for content.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
What is a partial?
Quarto does this for many parts of the page.


Same thing happens with other parts of the document: metadata, styles, etc.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
What is a partial?
Replace a partial without touching the rest of the template


Partition allows you to override a partial without touching the rest of the template. That’s what we’ll do today.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
Every release must carry:

the agency masthead
the reference period and the region
the release status — Provisional, Revised, or Final





this is a publishing requirement, not a design preference.
The same shape applies to any organization’s report template: fields that must appear on every document.

Add this line to title-block.html, right after <header ...>:

Exercise: 03-partials/01-masthead


 

Touch on review:

$variable$ substitutes a value
Any YAML key becomes a template variable. masthead is your key. Quarto has no masthead option and never reads it.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
Pandoc template syntax
Write in the format you are targeting: HTML here
Anything inside $...$ or ${...} is Pandoc’s template syntax.



Write
Get




$title$
the value of the title metadata key


$brs-release.period$
reach into nested metadata with a dot


$title-block.html()$
include a partial — the () mean a file



Pandoc’s template syntax →

The distinction that matters today: $name$ substitutes a value, $name.html()$ includes a file. Only the second is replaceable through template-partials.
$title$s works, but ${title}s is clearer — both give Hellos. The two forms are interchangeable everywhere, including partial calls and ${if(x)}…${endif}.
$$ matters the moment a partial contains a literal dollar — a price, or $(...) in a script.
Conditionals and loops are on the same page of the manual. We meet them in turns 3 and 4.

title: Build reusable structures
section: Your turn 2: add period and region
text:
Your turn 2: add period and region
Already in your YAML, and shown by nothing:


report.qmd

brs-release:
  period: "Q3 2026"
  region: Oregon



Copy, then complete, this line to title-block.html, below the subtitle’s $endif$:
<p class="report-period">______ · ______</p>
Render. What happens when you remove brs-release from report.qmd?



Exercise: 03-partials/02-period-and-region


 

After: delete region: and render. A separator with nothing after it — the bridge to turn 3.

title: Build reusable structures
text: Q3 2026 · Oregon, rendered exactly as written — unlike the date above it, which Quarto reformatted before the template ever saw it.

title: Build reusable structures
section: Your own metadata, your own namespace
text:
Your own metadata, your own namespace


report.qmd

masthead: _brand/brs-logo.svg   # our name at the top level
brs-release:                    # our name with names inside
  period: "Q3 2026"
  region: Oregon


Every top-level name you invent is a bet that Quarto will never claim it.


Nest, and you place that bet once instead of once per field.


The obvious name is logo. It’s taken — a real Quarto option in beamer, revealjs, typst and dashboards, free in format: html only.
Render this same file to typst with logo: set and Quarto puts the image in the page background itself. Module 04 picks this up.
masthead is safe. Nesting means you don’t have to know which names are.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
Condition markup on presence


title-block.html

$if(subtitle)$
<p class="subtitle lead">$subtitle$</p>
$endif$


Read as if subtitle has a value, then….


Prevents empty <p></p> in the document.


They’ve been rendering this since setup without reading it.
Pandoc has no comparison operator. $if(x)$ asks “does this have a value?” and nothing else — which is why a default has to live in the template.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
Your turn 3: add status


Add status: Provisional under brs-release: in report.qmd.
In title-block.html, below the reference period, show the status in a <span class="report-status"> — but only when brs-release.status is set.
Render. Then delete the status: line and render again — the badge should disappear, leaving nothing behind.



Exercise: 03-partials/03-release-status


 

No snippet, so the work is reading their own file and adapting it.
The assistant is a sanctioned escape hatch here.
After: status nests under brs-release: — the turn 2 rule, applied unprompted. The badge is unstyled and looks like nothing, which is the cue for turn 4.

title: Build reusable structures
text: Provisional as plain text. It carries the right information and reads like nothing, which is exactly the setup for turn 4: three classes in the markup, still no CSS.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
More Pandoc template syntax







Write
Get




$if(x)$ … $else$ … $endif$
conditionals


$for(x)$ … $endfor$
loop over an array


$sep$
inside a loop: emitted between items, never after the last


${x/uppercase}
a pipe — also lowercase, length, reverse, nowrap, …


$--
a comment, to the end of the line



Pandoc’s template syntax →

A signpost, not a lesson. You have met $if$; the rest is “this exists, the manual has it”.
$sep$ is worth ten seconds: a separator that knows it is between things.

title: Build reusable structures
section: For HTML: styling lives outside the partials
text:
For HTML: styling lives outside the partials


title-block.html

<span class="report-status">$brs-release.status$</span>


No color. No size. No position. Just a class.


Style using SCSS:


custom.scss

/*-- scss:rules --*/
.report-status { background-color: $primary; }



Three classes:report-masthead,report-period, report-status.


A partial decides what appears and in what order. A stylesheet decides what it looks like. Cross that line and nobody can restyle your template.
This is why the snippets shipped with class names already in them.

text:
Your turn 4: style what you built

Don’t edit title-block.html.

Ask Posit Assistant to style your title block. Start with the prompt below then describe what you want.

Example prompt:
I'm in @03-partials/04-style. Write SCSS to style my title block. Use our brand variables ($primary, $secondary, $brand-forest, $text-muted) and never a hard-coded color.

title: Build reusable structures
text:
Full or partial?

Replacing an entire template offers full control of output but comes with the risk of omitting required variables that can break Pandoc/Quarto features.
Safer approaches:

Selectively replace partials that exist within the master LaTeX or HTML template
Replace the entire LaTeX or HTML template, but then include partials provided with Quarto to ensure that your template takes advantage of all Pandoc and Quarto features

title: Build reusable structures
text:
Localized strings in templates
Hard-coding “Table of contents” in a partial breaks the moment someone sets lang:.
Since Quarto 1.10, the strings Quarto already translates are template variables:
<h2>${quarto.language.toc-title-document}</h2>




lang: en
lang: fr




Table of contents
Table des matières


Abstract
Résumé




Localized strings in templates →

The quarto.language namespace exposes every string Quarto localizes, resolved for the document’s lang.

title: Setup
text:
Accounts

GitHub account — needed to clone and work with the workshop materials. Sign up at https://github.com if you don’t have one.
Posit AI account — we’ll use Posit Assistant in Positron during the workshop. If you don’t already have one, create a free account at https://posit.ai. Use the same email address you registered for the workshop with, because this is how we attach your workshop credits.

title: Setup
text:
Software requirements

Positron
We’ll be live-coding in Positron. Download and install the latest Positron (2026.07 or newer) from https://positron.posit.co/download.
The following extensions are the ones we’ll be relying on and Positron already ships with them — nothing extra to install.

Quarto
Air
Posit Assistant

Quarto (latest release)
We’ll rely on recent features of Quarto, so please make sure you have the latest version installed — v1.10 or later. Check your version with:
quarto --version
Download at: https://quarto.org/docs/download/
R or Python
Bring whichever language you usually use with Quarto. For R, we recommend R 4.6 or later, an up-to-date tidyverse, and the quarto package (we use it for a few R-side rendering tricks):
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "quarto"))
Git
We’ll clone workshop materials and discuss version control workflows. If you don’t already have Git, install it from https://git-scm.com/downloads.
Posit AI
In Positron, open the Command Palette and run Authentication: Configure Language Model Providers, choose Posit AI, and sign in through your browser. That’s it! During the workshop, usage draws from the workshop’s credit pool first, not your personal balance.

title: Practical Quarto
text:
Instructors
Charlotte Wickham is a Senior Developer Advocate at Posit with a focus on Quarto. Before Posit, she taught Statistics and Data Science at Oregon State University. 
Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel is Professor of the Practice at Duke University in the Department of Statistical Science and Senior Developer Advocate at Posit, PBC, where she’s part of the tidyverse team. Mine is a co-author of influential open textbooks like R for Data Science and OpenIntro Statistics, and her contributions to education and open science have earned her several accolades, including the Waller Education Award by the American Statistical Association, the Robert V. Hogg Award by the Mathematical Association of America, and the Pickard Award by Harvard University’s Department of Statistics.

title: Practical Quarto
text:
Description
This workshop is designed for Quarto users who want to update and extend their Quarto mastery. Led by Charlotte Wickham and Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, this workshop will introduce new features of Quarto as well as blend practical recipes with conceptual understanding, so you can both copy–paste what works and understand why it works. Rather than a linear tour of Quarto features, the workshop is organized as a collection of focused, reusable patterns—each one solving a real authoring or publishing problem you’re likely to encounter.
Themes will include:

Work productively in Positron: Pick up Positron- and Quarto-specific productivity tips, including auto-formatting with Air, and practical ways to incorporate LLMs into your Quarto workflow.
Design once, use anywhere: Learn how to work effectively with light and dark modes, brands, and renderings, and how to share a consistent brand across multiple Quarto projects without duplication or fragility.
Build reusable structures: Use template partials to factor out repeated content and layouts, making large or long-lived projects easier to maintain and evolve.
Understand why Typst matters: Explore why Typst deserves a place on your radar, with concrete “quick wins” that show how it can dramatically simplify PDF generation.


By the end of the workshop, you’ll have a curated set of Quarto recipes and a mental model for how the pieces fit together. You’ll leave the workshop equipped to create more polished documents, scale your workflows across projects and teams, and make deliberate, informed choices about tools, formats, and authoring strategies.

text:
The same look, in how many places?

theme: — one SCSS file for html, another for revealjs
include-in-header: — fonts, again
mainfont:, colorlinks: — pdf has its own names
your plots — theme_*() in R, theme() in Python
and again in the next project


Five descriptions of one brand, each drifting on its own schedule.


The problem is not that any one of these is hard. It’s that there is no single place where the brand is written down.
This is the same shape as module 03 and 04: say it once, in the right place.

One file, written once, applied across Quarto formats — and beyond Quarto.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Two steps

Describe the brand in one _brand.yml.
Quarto applies it to almost every format.


No format-specific theming to write. No SCSS – unless you want to tweak bits of your document/website/slide deck brand doesn’t control via a YAML field.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Five keys

meta — who the brand belongs to: name, links
logo — the image files, at a few sizes
color — the palette, and the roles colors play
typography — fonts for base, headings, links, code
defaults — escape hatches for specific output formats


color and typography do most of the work. defaults is where you put the thing brand.yml has no word for.

  base:
    family: Atkinson Hyperlegible
    weight: 400

  headings:
    family: Atkinson Hyperlegible
    weight: 600

  link:
    color: primary
    decoration: underline



meta is documentation for humans only, Quarto doesn’t use it.
In logo, paths resolve relative to the brand file.
color works in two steps: name your colors in palette, then say what role each one plays, e.g., primary: forest, not primary: "#1b5e4f".

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Naming, then roles


_brand.yml

color:
  palette:
    forest: "#1b5e4f"   # a name for a hex code
  primary: forest       # a job for a name


In SCSS these arrive as $brand-forest and $primary.
In Typst these arrive as brand-color.primary.


This is the callback in both remaining modules — module 03’s custom.scss reaches for $primary and $brand-forest, module 04’s raw block for brand-color.primary.
Neither one hard-codes #1b5e4f. That is the payoff for writing the roles down.
The semantic list is longer than these two: secondary, tertiary, success, info, warning, danger, light, dark. In html and dashboard they land on the Bootstrap variables of the same name.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
defaults: the escape hatch


For the thing brand.yml has no word for:



_brand.yml

defaults:
  bootstrap:
    defaults:
      link-decoration: underline
      navbar-fg: "#fff"
    rules: |
      h2 {
        border: none;
      }




html and dashboard only.
Also takes uses, functions, mixins.



These are SCSS variables and rules, merged into the right layer of Quarto’s SCSS system.
This deck uses it: the h2 border rule is in our _brand.yml.
Reach for it last. Anything you can say in color or typography reaches all four formats; this reaches two.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Applying it

Save _brand.yml in the root of your project.
Render.


Quarto finds it, and applies it to every document in the project that supports it.





When it isn’t at the root: Use brand in a document or in _quarto.yml:


report.qmd

title: Regional Employment Indicators
format: html
brand: ../brand/brs.yml


When you want to turn it off: Use brand: false:


report.qmd

title: Regional Employment Indicators
format: html
brand: false



No key in the YAML. No line in _quarto.yml. The file’s location is the configuration.
Also works for a single document with no project around it — same directory is enough.
brand: takes a path — which means a brand can live outside the project. Hold that thought; the last section is about exactly this.
It also takes brand elements inline. Careful: doing that replaces the whole of _brand.yml, it does not merge with it.
false is the door out: one document that must not carry the brand.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Using brand values in document
Use the brand shortcode, {{< brand color primary >}} anywhere a value goes — a div attribute, a background color, inline text:



slides.qmd

## Findings {background-color="{{< brand color primary >}}"}


Learn more: https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/brand.html#using-brand-values


A shortcode, like {{< meta >}} in module 04 — resolved by Quarto, in the body, before Pandoc.
{{< brand logo mark >}} does the same for images.
Colors and logos only. typography, meta and defaults are not reachable this way.
Reach for it when Quarto hasn’t already wired the brand into the thing you’re styling.

title: Design once, use anywhere
section: Your turn 1: write a brand by hand
text:
Your turn 1: write a brand by hand

Exercise: 02-brand/01-first-brand





Render report.qmd first, so you have something to compare against.
Create _brand.yml in the same folder and name the agency’s colors:

color:
  palette:
    forest: "#1B5E4F"

Render. What happened?





Now give the colors jobs:

  foreground: ink
  primary: forest

Render. Then add typography with Atkinson Hyperlegible and render again.

More details in exercise README.
Once done, discuss with your neighbors: The palette colors are the agency’s. The role names are Quarto’s. Which of the two would you expect to change more often?

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Your turn 1: takeaways

No _quarto.yml, no theme:, no css:, no need to name _brand.yml in report.qmd, just place in the same directory.
Naming a color does nothing, assigning it does: palette names colors. The keys below it — foreground, background, primary, secondary — assign them.
background: white is a literal CSS color, not a palette name
source: google fetches the font at render time. base sets body text; headings sets every level of heading.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Two appearances, one document
Give theme a pair, and Quarto builds both:


_quarto.yml

format:
  html:
    theme:
      light: flatly
      dark: darkly


a toggle appears, top right
the one listed first is the default
respect-user-color-scheme: true defers to the reader’s OS or browser


This is the pre-brand version, and worth showing because the shape repeats: everything about light and dark is “give it two of something”.
Order matters. light first means light by default.
respect-user-color-scheme needs JavaScript; without it readers get the first one.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
One brand, two modes



Any color in color or typography takes a light/dark pair.
Colors in palette cannot take a pair — name the color once, choose per mode where the role is assigned.




_brand.yml

color:
  background:
    light: white
    dark: ink
  foreground:
    light: ink
    dark: sand

typography:
  headings:
    color:
      light: forest
      dark: sand



One file, both modes. This is the cheapest version and it covers most brands.
The limitation is the reason the palette/roles split matters: forest is one hex code in both modes, but which role it plays can differ.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Two brands, two modes
When the modes differ by more than color, split the files and define use brand field in either the YAML of your document or in _quarto.yml:


report.qmd

brand:
  light: brs-light.yml
  dark: brs-dark.yml


Same shape as theme, one level up.
Reach for this when typography or logos differ, not just colors.
In _quarto.yml this has to be file paths — inline brand metadata there is not supported yet.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Logos for both modes


For the project:


_brand.yml

logo:
  images:
    mark:
      path: brs-logo.svg
      alt: Bureau of Regional Statistics logo featuring a stylized bar chart
    mark-reversed:
      path: brs-logo-white.svg
      alt: Bureau of Regional Statistics logo featuring a stylized bar chart
  medium:
    light: mark
    dark: mark-reversed


Override for one document:


report.qmd

logo:
  light:
    path: large
    alt: Bureau of Regional Statistics logo featuring a stylized bar chart
  dark: brs-logo-white.svg



A dark logo is not a recolored light logo — that is why this is a separate file, not a filter.
images is where alt text lives. Name the image once, then use the name in small, medium, large.
Document-level logo: can name a brand resource (large), a file, or a pair.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Formats that can’t toggle
Some formats produce only one appearance and offer no toggle between light/dark:


Revealjs:


slides.qmd

format:
  revealjs:
    brand-mode: dark


Typst:


report.qmd

format:
  typst:
    brand-mode: dark



There is no runtime in a PDF and no toggle in a deck, so the choice moves to the YAML.
Worth saying out loud: a dark deck for a dark room is a real use case, and this is the one key that does it.
Both formats default to light, whatever order your brand lists.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Content for one mode only



light-content / .dark-content divs place the content in the same place, same size, so the layout doesn’t jump when the reader toggles.
{{< brand logo mark >}} already does this for you: it emits both, classed.




report.qmd


::: {.light-content}
![](brs-logo.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](brs-logo-white.svg)
:::



Under the hood: body carries .quarto-light or .quarto-dark, and CSS hides the other one.
The default variant for brand logo is both. Ask for light or dark explicitly and you get one, unclassed.
{{< brand color primary dark >}} is the same idea for colors — the third argument is the variant.

title: Design once, use anywhere
section: Your turn 2: one brand, two modes
text:
Your turn 2: one brand, two modes

Exercise: 02-brand/02-dark-mode





Give background, foreground and primary a value per mode:

  background:
    light: white
    dark: ink

Add respect-user-color-scheme: true to report.qmd, render, and switch your system appearance back and forth with the page open.





Look at the link to the methodology notes in dark mode. Fix it: add a lighter green to the palette and use it for the dark half of primary.

Stretch goal: Give secondary and tertiary mode values, then find something in the document that uses them, if any.
More details in exercise README.

Once done, discuss with your neighbors: The style guide gave you four colors and no dark mode. You invented mint. Is that a decision you are allowed to make, and who would you ask?

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Your turn 2: takeaways

Getting colors and color contrast right, especially in light/dark mode, requires careful review and iteration.
A standalone page, unlike a website, has no toggle in the corner;respect-user-color-scheme is how single pages use the dark stylesheet.

title: Design once, use anywhere
section: The plot didn’t get the memo
text: The plot didn’t get the memo

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Theme helpers
The quarto packages turn a brand into a plot theme:

RPython


library(quarto)

theme_set(theme_brand_ggplot2("_brand.yml"))


from quarto import theme_brand_plotnine

theme = theme_brand_plotnine("_brand.yml")





Helpers exist for ggplot2, plotnine, and others — same brand, so the plot matches the page without anyone picking a color.
The R helper applies theme_minimal() underneath, which you may or may not want.
One brand file in, one theme out. Which leaves the toggle unsolved.


R · Python

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Or read the brand yourself

RPython


library(brand.yml)

brand <- read_brand_yml("_brand.yml")
brand$color$primary


from brand_yml import Brand

brand = Brand.from_yaml("_brand.yml")
brand.color.primary




One source of truth, reachable from code.


For the case the helpers don’t cover: a hand-built figure, a table, a badge in a Shiny app.
Same rule as the SCSS variables — ask for the role, not the hex code.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Two modes need two plots

renderings says: this cell produces one output per mode.



report.qmd

```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
par(bg = "#FFFFFF", fg = "#000000")
plot(1:10)

par(bg = "#000000", fg = "#FFFFFF", col.axis = "#FFFFFF")
plot(1:10)
```



The number of outputs must match the number of renderings.



Quarto tags the outputs .light-content and .dark-content — the same mechanism as two slides ago, applied to computational output.
Two modes means two themes: build one from each brand file and emit a plot for each. Nothing here is automatic.
An image is baked at render time. This is the only way a plot follows the toggle.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
renderings + caption or crossref
renderings and fig-/tbl- labels don’t mix


Solution: Wrap the cell instead


report.qmd

::: {#fig-employment}

```{r}
#| label: employment-plot
#| renderings: [light, dark]
```

Non-farm payroll employment, by quarter

:::




Caution The cell’s label must not start with fig- or tbl-, the divs may


The div carries the crossref and the caption; the cell just makes the pictures.
Still label the cell — stable file names, and errors you can read.
This is the kind of gotcha worth knowing exists rather than memorizing.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Brand is the bottom layer
Suppose you have the following and a _brand.yml file in the directory:


_quarto.yml

format:
  html:
    theme: [cosmo, tweaks.scss]


Quarto reads this as:


_quarto.yml

format:
  html:
    theme: [brand, cosmo, tweaks.scss]   # brand is lowest priority



Want the brand to win? Say where it goes:


_quarto.yml

format:
  html:
    theme: [cosmo, brand, tweaks.scss]



This is the fragile one. A Bootswatch theme listed after brand quietly overrides your brand, and the file that did it never mentions the brand.
Your own SCSS goes last either way — module 03’s custom.scss sits on top of all of this.
If you are not combining with a Bootswatch theme, none of this matters.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Same trick, light and dark


_quarto.yml

format:
  html:
    theme:
      light: [cosmo, brand]
      dark: [slate, brand]


Two lists, each ordered. brand last in both, so the brand beats the theme in both modes.
Everything in this section is html and dashboard only — SCSS is a Bootstrap story.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Brand reaches four formats
html · dashboard · revealjs · typst







Key
Where it lands




foreground, background
body text and page, in all four


primary
links, navbar (html), progress bar (revealjs)


typography
base, headings, links, code


logo
navbar, sidebar, slide corner, page corner


defaults: bootstrap
html and dashboard only




Not pdf. Not docx. Not pptx. The brand.yml implementation is still growing — the docs mark the gaps with limitation callouts.
pdf missing is module 04’s whole argument: render to typst instead and the brand comes with you.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Logos land in different places
Set small, medium, large — Quarto picks per location:








Format
Location
Prefers




html, dashboard
top navbar
small › medium › large


html
side navigation
medium › small › large


revealjs
bottom right of slides
medium › small › large


typst
top left of the page
medium › small › large


website, book
browser tab favicon
small




You don’t have to set all three. One logo is fine until it looks wrong somewhere.
Turn it off per location in _quarto.yml — navbar: logo: false, sidebar: logo: false — when you want the colors but not the mark.
The gap module 03 fills: a standalone HTML document has no navbar, so the brand logo has nowhere to go.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Your turn 3: second format + logo

Exercise: 02-brand/03-both-formats





Add slides as a second format in report.qmd:

format:
  html:
    respect-user-color-scheme: true
  revealjs:
    output-file: slides.html

Preview each format, discuss with your neighbor how brand is applied.
Register brs-logo.svg in _brand.yml as mark; small and medium.



Preview each format, is logo there?
Insert logo it in report, above ## Summary:

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
{{< brand logo medium >}}
:::

Register brs-logo-white.svg too, and give both sizes a light/dark pair.

Once done, discuss with your neighbors: What if you only defined small, medium, or large for one of the logos?

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Your turn 3: takeaways

When both formats generate HTML, one of them need to output a filename that’s different than the name of the .qmd file, defined with output-file.
Not all formats use all inputs in _brand.yml, e.g., HTML documents don’t get a logo by default, but elements defined in _brand.yml can be called explicitly with the brand shortcode.
content-hidden when-format="revealjs" is conditional content – keeps the shortcode out of the deck, which already has the logo in the corner.
The brand shortcode emits two <img> tags, light-content and dark-content.

title: Design once, use anywhere
section: A brand is a file, so it can be a repo
text:
A brand is a file, so it can be a repo

one brand, several projects — a website, a report, a deck, an app
edited in one place, by whoever owns the brand
versioned, so a change is a commit and not a surprise


The catch: Quarto needs the assets inside your project. Logos and font files can’t be referenced across the filesystem or the network.


So “share” means “copy, and keep the copy in sync”. Say that plainly — it sounds like a compromise until you consider a font file that vanishes mid render.
Commit the copies. A brand you can’t rebuild from a clone is not shared.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
quarto use brand


Terminal

quarto use brand ./brand-repo         # a local directory
quarto use brand myorg/shared-brand   # a GitHub repository
quarto use brand https://example.com/brand.zip


Copies into _brand/, then makes it match the source: it asks before creating the directory, before overwriting a file, and before removing one the source no longer has.




Terminal

quarto use brand myorg/shared-brand --dry-run   # show me first
quarto use brand myorg/shared-brand --force     # no prompts, for CI



Quarto 1.9. Re-run it to pick up changes to the shared brand — that is the sync story, and it is one command.
--dry-run prints would-overwrite / would-create / would-remove. Use it the first time on a project you care about.
--force trusts the source and answers every prompt yes. Fine in a workflow, not at a terminal.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Or a brand extension


_extensions/

_extensions/
  myorg/
    brs-brand/


installs like any other Quarto extension
update with quarto update
distributed from a Git repository

Brand extensions →

Same idea, different plumbing: still a copy in your project, tracked as an extension instead of a _brand/ directory.
Pick one and be consistent. Two copies of a brand in one project is the fragility we’re trying to avoid.

title: Design once, use anywhere
section: Your turn 4: stop writing the brand
text:
Your turn 4: stop writing the brand

Exercise: 02-brand/04-shared-brand



Delete the brand you wrote, and both SVGs.
Preview the report without the brand to remind yourself what it looks like without it.
Change the directory to the exercise folder, then take the agency’s brand — with --dry-run first, then without:

quarto use brand posit-conf-2026/practical-quarto-exercises/brs-brand --dry-run

Look at what landed in _brand/, preview both formats.
Switch your system appearance to dark, what happens?

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Your turn 4: takeaways

If the brand isn’t what you want, do not fix that by editing _brand/_brand.yml. Instead, fix the source and run quarto use brand again.
quarto use brand takes a local directory, a GitHub org/repo, an org/repo/path within one, or a URL to a zip. It copies files into _brand/.
--dry-run shows what would happen, without changing anything.
--force skips the prompts, which is what you might want if not working interactively, e.g., in a CI workflow.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
One brand, every page
A _brand.yml in the project root applies to the whole site:

Each page gets the brand’s colors and typography.
Navbar gets primary and the logo, in small size.
Browser tab gets the favicon.
theme: brand is not required if no other theme is listed, but it is useful if the brand is built on a Bootswatch theme – same layering rule as before.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Dark mode comes built in

Websites get a light/dark toggle in the navbar automatically when the theme has two halves:



_quarto.yml

format:
  html:
    theme:
      light: brand
      dark: brand



With light/dark pairs in _brand.yml, the toggle flips the whole site, including navbar, links, code, and logo.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Your turn 5: brand the website

Exercise: 02-brand/05-website





Change the directory to the exercise folder, bring the shared brand into the website project, then render the site:

quarto use brand posit-conf-2026/practical-quarto-exercises/brs-brand

Set the navbar to the brand color:

website:
  navbar:
    background: primary

Render again and find everywhere the brand shows up: navbar, links, headings, favicon.





Give the site a light/dark toggle with theme: light: brand, dark: brand, and flip it.
Does the navbar logo stay readable in both modes? Remember: don’t edit the copy in _brand/ — what would you ask the brand owner for instead?

Stretch goal: Add a page that doesn’t exist yet — how much branding work does the new page take?

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Your turn 5: takeaways

In a website project, _brand.yml applies site-wide — pages, navbar, and favicon — with no per-page configuration.
Websites get a built-in light/dark toggle; with light/dark pairs in the brand, the whole site (including the navbar logo) follows it.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Reaching brand values from code







Where
How




SCSS
$brand-forest, $primary


Typst
brand-color.primary, brand-logo-images.mark.path


Markdown
{{< brand color primary dark >}}, {{< brand logo mark >}}


R
read_brand_yml("_brand.yml")


Python
Brand.from_yaml("_brand.yml")


Lua filter
require('modules/brand/brand'), brand.get_color('primary')




The Lua row is for the workshop we point at in the wrap-up — a filter can read the brand too.

title: Design once, use anywhere
text:
Learn more

Multiformat branding with _brand.yml — the semantic color list, the typography fields, every limitation callout
brand.yml — the specification, and the other tools that read it
Dark mode — the toggle, respect-user-color-scheme, mode-specific content
Cell renderings — renderings: [light, dark]
More about Quarto themes — the SCSS layers, if you need to know what beats what

title: Why Typst matters
text:
Same release, new requirement
The Bureau of Regional Statistics quarterly release. Every one must carry:

the agency mark
the reference period and the region
the release status — Provisional, Revised, or Final


Last module we built all three into an HTML title block. Now it has to be a PDF.


Do not sell Typst yet. Get them to render one first.
The starter is the document without the title block work — a clean sheet, not their module 03 folder.

title: Why Typst matters
section: Your turn 1: render it as a PDF
text:
Your turn 1: render it as a PDF


Add typst as a second format in report.qmd. Keep html:


report.qmd

format:
  html: default
  typst: default

Render with Quarto: Preview Format… command and pick Typst.
Render the HTML too. Compare the two formats.



Exercise: 04-typst/01-first-pdf


 

No TeX install.
Quarto: Preview Format… — the command from this morning.
Add, don’t replace. They end holding both outputs, which is what makes step 3 possible.
Steer the comparison to the logo, and to the status with nothing marking it.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
Same brand in both: Atkinson Hyperlegible, brand ink for the text, forest links.
The logo only shows up in the PDF. Brand cannot place it in a standalone HTML document — module 03 built a partial for exactly that. Here it arrives with no configuration.
The date is 2026-09-14 here and September 14, 2026 in the HTML.
{{< meta brs-release.status >}} in the Summary works in both.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
Why Typst?

Already installed. format: pdf needs a LaTeX distribution. Typst ships inside Quarto.
Faster. Render, look, change, look again.
Uses your brand. Colors, fonts, and the logo, from the same _brand.yml.


Typst is a binary dependency, in the same quarto check list as Pandoc.
Brand reaches none of this in LaTeX. The .tex has no trace of it.
Headings are brand ink here, not primary. Turn 3 changes that.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
Two ways to reach metadata









Last module
This module




Where you write it
title-block.html, a partial
report.qmd, the body


What you write
$brs-release.status$
{{< meta brs-release.status >}}


What it is
Pandoc template syntax
a Quarto shortcode




Pandoc’s template syntax only runs when Pandoc is filling a template.

Pandoc’s template syntax →
Quarto’s meta shortcode →

$brs-release.status$ typed in the body is just text.
Both reach a nested key with a dot.
The shortcode also works inside a raw Typst block too.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
.qmd → .typ → .pdf






Keep the intermediate .typ:


report.qmd

format:
  typst:
    keep-typ: true



Two renders, not one. Pandoc gets you to Typst; Typst gets you to PDF.
The middle file is normally deleted. Keep it and you can read it, and errors point into it.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
Your content translated to Typst


report.typ

= Summary
<summary>
This is a Provisional release covering Oregon for the reference period Q3 2026.

Total employment in the region rose by 4,300 jobs over the quarter, an increase of 0.4%. Sector detail is in #ref(<tbl-sectors>, supplement: [Table]), and the full method is in the #link("https://example.gov/brs/methods")[methodology notes].

#strong[All figures in this release are #emph[provisional].]

#quote(block: true)[
Benchmarking aligns the survey estimates with the annual census of employment.
]


Template contributes 431 lines above it…


Every line above 432 came from the template and its partials, or from the brand.
475 lines in total for a two-page release.
Scroll up through it live. Do not read it out — just show the scale, then land on #show: doc => article( and brand-color.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
Template: format: typst


The boilerplate, in order. Their content is the box in the middle.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
Text is content




badge.typ

Provisional





A .typ starts in markup mode. Text is text.
= is a heading, - a list item. Typst has *bold* and _italic_ too — Pandoc just does not use them.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
# switches into code




badge.typ

rect()






badge.typ

#rect()









Empty parentheses: a call with no arguments.

Typst: rect →

One character is the whole difference. Without the # you get the characters rect() back as text.
The docs page for rect is the next two slides, ahead of time.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
Arguments go in the parentheses




badge.typ

#rect(fill: green)





Named arguments. A function’s reference page is a list of these.
green is built in.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
Use [] to pass content arguments




badge.typ

#rect(fill: green)[Provisional]





This is the same call:
#rect(fill: green, [Provisional])

Typst: trailing content blocks →

[...] is a content block. The box now has something in it.
Typst calls the [...] after the parentheses a trailing content block, and you will see both spellings in the docs.
With nothing else in the parentheses they can go too: #rect[Provisional]. A function can even take several trailing blocks — #enum(start: 2)[A][B].

title: Why Typst matters
text:
Your turn 2: read the Typst


Render, then open report.typ. Scroll down to = Summary — everything below it is your content.
Find a call — it starts with #.
Search for the function in the Typst reference. Say in plain words what it does, and whether any arguments are being passed to it.
Again, with another one.



Exercise: 04-typst/02-read-the-typ


 

All four are in the first section: #ref, #link, #quote, and a #strong with an #emph nested inside it.
Arguments vary on purpose — #strong takes none, #quote(block: true) takes a named one, #link and #ref take one unnamed and then content.
Collect two or three out loud. The reference being readable is the point, not finishing.

title: Why Typst matters
section: You can nest content and calls
text:
You can nest content and calls




badge.typ

#rect(fill: green)[
  #text(fill: white)[Provisional]
]





They just met this in their own file — #strong[... #emph[provisional] ...].
Inside [...] you are back in content mode, so the second # does the same job as the first.
This is the shape the status badge needs.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
Writing Typst in a .qmd
A raw block passes straight through:


report.qmd


title: Why Typst matters
Why Typst matters
text:
Every element has a function
Even if not explicitly called, all layout and styling happens with functions:







Element
Its function




Text
text()


Heading
heading()


Paragraphs
par()


Page
page()




Nothing is exempt. Provisional on its own is a text element — we just never named the function.
Typst’s own word for these is element function, and its docs say every one of them can be customised with set and show rules. That is the next two slides.
Their .typ already has set par, set text, set heading and set page, all written by Quarto from the YAML and the brand.

#show heading: set text(fill: brand-color.primary)

= Summary

Ordinary text here

== Manufacturing





A show-set rule: the show keyword, a selector, a colon, then a set rule.

Typst: styling →

Read it as: wherever a heading appears, apply this.
Nothing had to be marked up — show finds the elements itself.

title: Why Typst matters
text:
.where() narrows the selector




styles.typ

#show heading.where(level: 1): set text(fill: brand-color.primary)

= Summary
== Manufacturing





Same rule, narrower selector. heading.where(level: 1) is still the heading function, with a filter on it.
Careful: Quarto shifts levels down by one, so a markdown ## is Typst level 1.

section: When a raw block is not enough
text:
When a raw block is not enough







You want
Reach for




rules used across documents
include-before: styles.typ


a header or footer on every page
override page.typ


a different title block
override typst-show.typ, typst-template.typ




A raw block styles what is already there. It cannot touch the title block — that is built before your content arrives.
#set page() in the body starts a new page too, so a body raw block cannot even reach page one.

title: Why Typst matters
section: Seed with the defaults, hand to an agent
text:
Seed with the defaults, hand to an agent
I've added page.typ, typst-show.typ and typst-template.typ, 
unedited copies of Quarto's Typst partials, already registered in report.qmd. 
Edit the partials to rebuild the title block: 
title and subtitle alongside a right aligned the brand logo, 
the reference period and region, 
then the release status as a badge. 

Do not ask for partials from scratch — it will drop the machinery behind cross-references, footnotes and the bibliography.
page.typ is the interesting change: a deletion. Editing a partial is as often about removing default behaviour as adding to it.
The logo comes from _brand.yml, not a document key. $logo$ on its own renders the string true; you want $logo.path$.
Brand colours are not template variables — only brand.typography.* is. brand-color is a Typst variable, so pass it from typst-show.typ.

Tinymist Typst — syntax highlighting and completion for .typ files.
myriad-dreamin.tinymist
Open VSX · VS Code Marketplace · Docs

Positron installs extensions from Open VSX, and this one is there.
It covers .typ files. A {=typst} raw block inside a .qmd is not highlighted — the grammar only injects into fences labelled typ or typst.
nvarner.typst-lsp is the predecessor and contributes no grammar. Uninstall it if you have both.
